I work on Sengi, a hosted runner service for GitHub Actions, and the Sengi rows below are ours. GitHub's figures are its published per-minute rates and included minutes, the ones in effect since January 1, 2026. Every line of arithmetic is on the page.
A GitHub Actions bill has two numbers in it: the minutes and the price per minute. Most advice goes after the minutes: cache more, skip jobs, split suites. All good. But both numbers are also set by the machine your job runs on, and that's the lever this post is about.
Take last month's job-minutes.
On standard runners in private repositories, subtract your plan's included minutes: 2,000 on GitHub Free, 3,000 on Pro and Team, 50,000 on Enterprise Cloud.
Multiply what's left by the runner's rate: $0.006 a minute for Linux 2-core, $0.012 for 4…

articles.author: Naman Gupta
articles.description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady
🦥 SlothSort — A Sloth-Themed File Organizer
SlothSort is a web application designed to make file organization simpler and less tedious. The goal is to help users spend less time manually organizing files and explore how AI could make the process easier.
Try the live application:
https://sloth-sort-flow.base44.app
Explore the source code on GitHub:
https://github.com/namangupta-prog/SlothSort
I built SlothSort using Base44 and a React-based frontend.
I also explored Ollama integration to investigate using open-weight AI models for file-organization suggestions. However, I haven't connected and tested a real model yet, so local AI inference remains unfinished.
Open innovation gives developers the freedom to explore models and tools beyond closed, hosted AI APIs.
For SlothSort, a properly configured local model could eventually provide more control over how file information is processed and allow experimentation with different models. This project is an early step toward exploring those possibilities.
I haven't published an agent session for this project yet.
SlothSort aims to reduce the repetitive effort involved in organizing files. I haven't measured time savings with real users yet, so testing the workflow and measuring its benefits are future goals.
Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.
I'll add any applicable partner prize categories after verifying their requirements.


  
  
  hf26challenge #hacktoberfest #opensource #ai
articles.title: SlothSort 🦥: A Slow and Steady Approach to AI-Powered File Organization

articles.author: Dr Srinivas Padmanabhuni
articles.description:
Clone agentest: run agentic AI checklist tests offline in CI


Shipping agents that plan → call tools → hand off → mutate state? Chat review and LLM-as-judge miss a lot of failures: false completion, wrong tool order, privacy leaks, biased labels, flaky plans.
agentest is an Apache-2.0 open-core runner for the Agentic AI Test Checklist 110. Clone it and run — no Hugging Face account required at runtime.
git clone https://github.com/srpadmanabhuni/agentest.git
cd agentest
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
agentest samples
agentest run --suite functional --agent golden
agentest run --suite orchestration --agent golden
agentest matrix

Suites: functional, privacy, explainability, bias_fairness, orchestration
15 sample agents (10 green ladder + 5 expected-fail teaching scenarios)
Deterministic oracles against a mock tool gateway
ISO 42001 / assurance-taxonomy aligned checklist design (not certification)
Pulse: Testing Agentic AI

Zenodo taxonomy: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23587407

Developer guide: https://github.com/srpadmanabhuni/agentest/blob/main/docs/DEVELOPER-GUIDE.md



Author: Dr Srinivas Padmanabhuni · srinivas AT testAIng.com
articles.title: Clone agentest: run agentic AI checklist tests offline in CI

There is a gap between a CVSS score and a threat actor's willingness to use a bug, and CVE-2025-61624 is a clean example. NVD records the vulnerability at 6.0 under CVSS v3.1, medium severity. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 16 October 2026 with a remediation deadline of 19 October. Palo Alto Networks attributes its use to a cluster tracked as UNC5820 and CL-STA-0954, which deployed ARM64 malware named PeerStitch against telecommunications targets.
